https://www.politico.eu/article/nigel-fa.text: LONDON — On the ropes, Nigel Farage is going for a right hook. The Reform UK leader — who has faced intense pressure over his finances over the summer — came out swinging Monday at a Westminster press conference focused on his core issue: borders. Reform is pushing plans for a military drive — dubbed “Operation Fortress” — which it claims would ensure no small boat carrying undocumented migrants reaches the English coastline. Advertisement Advertisement Under its proposals, an “integrated surveillance command” to track boats using drones, space satellites and infrared feeds would be established using the Royal Navy, Royal Air Force, Royal Marines and British Army. Small boats would be intercepted at sea with their occupants detained, medically-assessed and given food and water before being returned on military inflatable boats to the country they came from, most likely France. “I am entirely confident that under a Reform government, within a fortnight, there would be no more boats,” Farage — who took questions at a press conference for the first time since early May — told reporters. “If the Royal Navy is not there to protect this country from invasion, then, frankly, I can’t see what its purpose is,” he added. Seizing the agenda The Reform announcement comes as the ruling Labour Party enjoys a modest bounce in opinion polls two weeks after swapping out Keir Starmer as prime minister for former Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham. Burnham has seized the agenda, announcing a flurry of spending commitments in his first fortnight in charge, and struck a more optimistic tone than his predecessor. Advertisement Advertisement He also moves into No. 10 Downing Street with the salience of immigration slightly diminished. The number of people arriving in the U.K. on small boats was 43 percent lower between Jan. 1 and Aug. 1 this year compared to last year. But Savanta’s Political Research Director Chris Hopkins explained that immigration remains a top issue for voters. “It is important Burnham doesn’t ignore the issue given its general importance in U.K. politics,” he said. Hopkins adds that “getting the tone right is a tricky tightrope for a Labour prime minister to walk,” especially with the risk of turning off potential Labour-to-Green switchers on the left. Easier said than done Burnham has so far tried to show he’s on the front foot on migration. He has retained Shabana Mahmood as home secretary, one of the few holdovers from the Starmer era and a figure who has riled up some on the Labour left with more stringent immigration rules. Shabana Mahmood arrives in Downing Street, London on Dec. 9, 2025. | Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing via Getty Images During a visit to Dover over the weekend, Burnham — with the famous white cliffs in the background — promised a “relentless” focus on small boat crossings. “People want to see this issue addressed,” the prime minister said. “The public don’t like the idea that the border looks like it’s not controlled. We need to bring back that control, but also we need to offer support for people who genuinely need it,” he added. Advertisement Advertisement Labour MP Sojan Joseph, whose Ashford constituency is near the Kent coast where many small boats arrive, praised Burnham’s approach so far — though argued that more action is needed. “We must continue the positive work we’ve already done to reduce the number of small boat crossings and to close asylum hotels, with the hotel in my constituency already closed, to restore order to our borders — and deliver where the previous Tory government failed,” Joseph said. On Monday, Burnham’s official spokesperson dismissed Reform’s proposals, insisting the Royal Navy already has “primacy for small boat crossings” and that border patrol officers have “significant capabilities and skills that make them the best suited candidate to lead small boats operations in the channel.” In a BBC interview, former navy commander Tom Sharpe also questioned whether the Royal Navy has the capability to enforce Farage’s plans. Reform is “talking about the largest maritime operation in the Channel since World War Two, a very evocative image, but that’s not the reality,” he said. Reform has also faced a host of questions about what it would do if France rejects the small boats that have been turned around and sent back to its coastline. Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesman, said France would be committing a “crime against humanity” if it ordered French forces to block a “humanitarian mission landing civilians in safety and forcing them back out to sea, directly endangering their lives.” Battle of the narratives Beyond questions about its viability, Farage’s success will depend on whether he can keep attention on this policy — and away from the multiple controversies surrounding his party. Advertisement Advertisement Farage is facing a special election in his seaside seat of Clacton next week, which he has billed as a chance for the public to show it is unfazed by “establishment” scrutiny of a £5 million gift he received from a cryptocurrency investor before the last election. Shortly before the Reform press conference kicked off Monday, the parliamentary standards watchdog confirmed it is separately investigating the party’s Deputy Leader Richard Tice over an allegation he failed to declare an interest. The Reform UK leader is also facing pressure on his right flank from Rupert Lowe’s rival Restore Britain outfit. Farage faced questions Monday about the potential for an alliance with Lowe’s breakaway party, which continues to poll in the single digits but threatens to split the vote on the right. The Reform UK chief said he would “do whatever I could for us to have a sane center-right alliance to beat Labour at the next general election” — though Lowe has continued to direct social media barbs at Farage in the hours since the press conference. Right-wing splits aside, Farage will be hoping he can keep the political conversation on his terms — and not Burnham’s.

https://www.politico.eu/article/ireland-.text: DUBLIN — Ireland is girding itself to offer U.S. President Donald Trump the country’s legendary “hundred thousand welcomes” — and, privately, cannot wait for him to leave. The official Irish priorities ahead of Trump’s arrival Saturday are to keep protesters out of sight and keep the president’s focus on the Irish Open golf tournament being played at his resort on the west coast. “He invited himself to Ireland to see the golf. That’s grand. We need to get him through Dublin as smoothly and trouble-free as possible. Smiling faces, nice pictures, no friction,” a senior Irish government official said. Advertisement Advertisement The official spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the behind-the-scenes preparations for a trip that has been on Ireland’s radar since St. Patrick’s Day nearly six months ago. When Taoiseach Micheál Martin visited the White House , he agreed with Trump that he probably should visit his County Clare resort in remote Doonbeg this weekend as it hosts the country’s premier golf tournament. Once Trump’s Qatari-donated Air Force One lands at Dublin Airport, he’s expected to be flown by Marine One helicopter into Phoenix Park , a vast urban oasis that was once the hunting grounds for the British ruling elite — and today provides an ideal one-stop shop for diplomacy behind easily secured walls. Confining Trump to the Phoenix Park has meant shutting down one of the biggest urban parks in Europe , including one of Dublin’s top tourist attractions, the zoo, since Thursday night. But it also sidestepped the U.S. government’s initial wish to have the center of Dublin shut down so Trump could visit the future site of a new American embassy. That had been the hope of Trump’s ambassador to Ireland , a New Jersey property developer and avid golfer named Edward Walsh. “A groundbreaking ceremony in the middle of the capital would have been a security and logistical nightmare,” the Irish official said. It’s still going to take an estimated 4,000 security personnel — including a reported 1,000 U.S. Secret Service agents and other American security staff operating anti-drone weaponry — to keep protesters and any would-be assassins out of range when Trump meets Irish leaders in Phoenix Park before flying across to Doonbeg. Advertisement Advertisement Dan Mulhall, who was Ireland’s ambassador to the U.S. during Trump’s first term, said the decision to award the Irish Open to Trump’s resort made this weekend’s tricky diplomacy inevitable. “There will be relief in [the Irish] government when it’s over,” he said. “I am sure they don’t fancy the visit but it has to be done.” Ever since Trump’s return to power, the Irish government’s key objective has been to limit any attacks on the exceptional role that U.S. drug and tech companies play in fueling Ireland’s EU-leading economy. “We depend on the U.S. for so much, there’s no getting away from that critical fact. We do offer a lot in return, and we’ll be keen to reinforce that point. So naturally, while he’s here, President Trump will be guaranteed the full céad míle fáilte ,” the Irish official said, using a native phrase proclaiming “a hundred thousand welcomes.” U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to Taoiseach of Ireland Micheál Martin during a meeting in the Oval Office of the White House on March 17, 2026. | Alex Wong/Getty Images Phoenix Park is home to three of the grandest venues for Irish diplomacy: Farmleigh House , a former retreat for the Guinness brewing dynasty and the state’s official guesthouse for visiting dignitaries; U.S. Ambassador Walsh’s Deerfield residence ; and Áras an Uachtaráin, the home of Ireland’s ceremonial head of state, President Catherine Connolly. Trump will visit Walsh first, then Connolly at her place, and finally Martin at Farmleigh. Irish confidence is running high that the ultra-polite Martin can swerve any awkward moments, given how he emerged unscathed from two St. Patrick’s Day visits to the White House. But nails are being bitten over Trump’s encounter with Connolly, a socialist opposition politician who often denounced Trump before her election last year as head of state, a non-government role designed to articulate Irish values, not policy. Connolly, an ardent supporter of the Palestinian people, personally protested Trump’s first presidential visit to Ireland in 2019. Before her presidential win, Connolly was an early and frequent critic of Trump , once declaring: “I have difficulty calling him ‘President Trump’.” Advertisement Advertisement For his part, Trump incorrectly presumed, during his only public comments about Connolly, that she was a man. For their first face-to-face meeting, Connolly’s team is strictly limiting who can attend the official handshake and greeting inside the Áras. Unlike previous U.S. presidential visits , Trump isn’t expected to join the Irish president in ringing a symbolic peace bell outside. Likewise, whereas previous U.S. presidents have addressed the joint houses of Ireland’s parliament, an honor most recently bestowed on Biden in 2023 , the building will remain closed for Trump’s visit. “We have the convenient excuse that it’s a weekend,” said the Irish official, who conceded that the parliament has observed exceptional recalls from holiday periods to celebrate Biden and other visiting U.S. presidents. “We never got the impression that this was something President Trump was particularly keen to do anyway.” Thousands of left-wing protesters, including senior figures from the main opposition party, Sinn Féin , are expected to march through central Dublin while Trump stays in the park. Anti-Trump protesters plan similar demonstrations Sunday in rural County Clare on the final day of the Irish Open, where the national police force and U.S. Secret Service have spent weeks wargaming how best to keep them far from the fairways. Within the security cordon, Trump seems assured of a warm welcome from Doonbeg’s economically minded locals . They express uniform admiration for a U.S. leader who snapped up the bankrupt local resort at a knock-down price in 2014 and, spearheaded by son Eric , has transformed it into the area’s top employer and a highly profitable venture . Similarly, the golfing elite — led by defending Irish Open champion Rory McIlroy — say they see only good coming from a chance to share a spotlight with Trump. “We are all happy to be here, grateful to be here, and his [Trump’s] presence at the Irish Open makes it a truly international event,” McIlroy told a Doonbeg press conference. “That brings more attention and eyeballs, and that can only be a good thing.” Advertisement Advertisement

Photograph: gorodenkoff/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Analysis of the first patients to use the service shows some are as young as 13, with most being girls and most living in deprived areas. Photograph: gorodenkoff/Getty Images Drugs Children as young as 13 being referred to UK hospital suffering from ‘ketamine bladder’ County’s first such clinic, at Alder Hey in Liverpool, treating children suffering from chronic bladder problems with severe cases needing dialysis Andrew Gregory Health editor Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Children as young as 13 in the UK have been referred to a specialist clinic for a “devastating” bladder condition linked to sustained use of ketamine. Medics at Alder Hey children’s hospital in Liverpool opened the first ketamine clinic in the UK for young people amid a surge in urology problems linked to addiction of the drug. Now analysis of the first patients to use the service shows some are as young as 13, with most being girls and most living in deprived areas. Excessive use of ketamine can cause serious health problems as the drug and its breakdown products sit in the bladder for a long time, where they can damage the lining and muscle tissue. Ketamine-induced uropathy – also known as ketamine bladder – is a severe and painful condition caused by the drug damaging the bladder, urinary tubes and kidneys. Symptoms include frequent urination, loss of bladder control and blood in the urine. View image in fullscreen Ketamine use can damage the bladder wall, causing ulceration and fibrosis, say experts. Photograph: Joe Bird/Alamy Some of the children affected are using incontinence pads and urinating in buckets next to their bed at night due to bladder problems caused by addiction to ketamine. “The damage caused by ketamine can be devastating,” said Harriet Corbett, a consultant paediatric urologist at Alder Hey children’s NHS foundation trust. “It can affect the bladder wall, causing ulceration and fibrosis, and the effects can be irreversible. Young people can experience chronic bladder pain and incontinence and, in the most severe cases, may go on to require major surgery or dialysis.” Doctors were being referred to a rising number of children with bladder symptoms caused by non-prescribed ketamine use, Corbett added. “What this first year of analysis has highlighted is the importance of understanding the young person behind the diagnosis.” Analysis of the first patients to use the service shows some are as young as 13, with most being girls and most living in deprived areas. “By looking at factors such as age, where they live, their background and their life experiences, we can start to build a much clearer picture of who is being affected and how we can best support them. “This problem is preventable. Understanding more about the young people who are presenting to us is an important step towards preventing further harm,” Corbett said. View image in fullscreen Alder Hey children’s hospital has opened the UK’s first ketamine clinic for young people. Photograph: Mark Waugh/Alamy Analysis of the clinic’s first 60 patients by researchers at Alder Hey and Lancaster University showed their average age was 14, ranging from 13 to 15. About two-thirds were girls, and roughly the same proportion lived in the most deprived areas, according to the analysis published in the Archives of Disease in Childhood medical journal. Of the 60, 16 had autism or ADHD, or both. One in five had experience of the care system. Almost three-quarters (72%) had experienced emotional trauma during childhood. The agony of ketamine addiction: ‘I felt like I was peeing glass’ Read more Prof Rachel Isba, a consultant in paediatric public health medicine at Alder Hey and professor emerita of children and young people’s health at Lancaster University, said: “One of the most important things about this work is that we are trying to understand the wider picture. “Ketamine use does not happen in isolation, and our analysis is helping us explore the different factors that may be associated with young people developing serious health problems.” The clinic at Alder Hey takes a “non-judgmental” approach, Isba said. “We want to give young people a safe space to talk about what is happening in their lives and work with them to develop a plan to stop using ketamine and prevent further damage.” Explore more on these topics Drugs Children Health Young people Poverty Hospitals Autism news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/07/us-l.text: US military carried out what it said were limited new airstrikes in southern Iran on Friday night, further raising fears across the Middle East and among Gulf states sparked by the possible resumption of an all-out war, but Qatar and the US insisted that the negotiations for a diplomatic settlement are continuing.US President Donald Trump told the media on Friday evening that a “minor” military action targeted Iranian air defence systems on Qeshm Island.“They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five," Trump said.Trump insisted that “we are not fighting” and made it clear that in parallel with the “minor strike,” the US has made “a lot of progress with Iran” with the ongoing negotiations spearheaded by chief mediator Qatar.“We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal,” Trump said.Iranian state-run media reported that two missiles hit the Suza area of Qeshm Island without identifying the targets or the damage, while locals went on social media reporting the explosions.Earlier on Friday, the Iranian Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) claimed that it shot down a US military drone over southern Iran, but the US did not confirm the claim.Friday’s strike is the first since the Democratic Party scored a major victory in midterm elections, with officials and analysts tying the result to voters' disagreement with Trump’s decision to enter into a war with Iran.The attack follows another series of what the US military called defensive strikes on Monday, when explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam in the Strait of Hormuz and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.In an earlier speech in Florida on Friday, Trump appeared to defend his Iran war decision by stating that “if I allowed Iran to have a nuclear weapon, today there would be no Israel,” and that “Israel would have been wiped off the face of the Earth.”Qatar presents new proposals to Iranian officialsQatar rushed to deny conflicting reports circulating on Friday night about the purported collapse of the negotiations, insisting in a statement that “Qatari mediators remain in close coordination with the United States and Iran to support ongoing negotiations.”Earlier on Friday, two Middle East government officials told AP that Iran was reviewing proposals presented by Qatar aimed at addressing differences with the US about Tehran’s nuclear program.But one of the officials stressed that the Iranians, at least at the moment, remain unwilling to engage in negotiations with the Trump administration over their atomic activities until the US agrees to several core conditions that Iran has been demanding be part of any ceasefire agreement, according to the AP.Differences with Iran over its nuclear program remain the thorniest issue, and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the more than eight-month-long war.Tehran insists on several concessions from the US which Trump has declined in the past. Among the core demands Iran says must be met before engaging in nuclear talks are the ending of the US military blockade on Iran’s ports, lifting sanctions, unfreezing its assets, issuing compensation for war damage and ending hostilities throughout the region, including Israeli military operations in Lebanon.Meanwhile, a flurry of diplomatic phone calls between leaders in the Gulf and beyond indicates intense efforts to prevent the resumption of an all-out war which would have devastating consequences for the region.Trump called Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani on Friday night to discuss “the ongoing diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalating tensions in the region (and) to pave the road for reaching a comprehensive agreement that resolves the crisis and ensures security and stability in the region,” according to Qatar’s national news agency.“In this regard, His Highness emphasised the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes, preventing further escalation in the region, and safeguarding freedom of maritime navigation and the security of energy supplies,” the statement said.Also on Friday, US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth spoke with his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, according to the Qatari government.In parallel, Qatar’s Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani told an Oxford University event on Friday that “for the past couple of weeks, we have worked with colleagues in the US administration who have very genuine intentions to find a way to contain the situation and de-escalate it,” as this crisis “cannot be left unresolved”.He insisted that the ongoing negotiations aim “to prevent the situation from spiralling out of control,” and that “thanks also to some wise voices in Tehran, we have prevented that from getting out of control”.“We will never have a perfect peace deal, but we cannot just wait for this moment of a perfect deal and avoid having a good deal,” Qatar’s prime minister said. "Our engagement did not stop and will not stop.”Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he also held phone calls with no less than 12 foreign ministers over the last two days to explain Iran’s “fundamental positions".In an Instagram post, Araghchi called for “regional security arrangements without the interference of superregional powers”.Iran’s military continued its threatening rhetoric on Saturday, with army spokesman Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia warning that “we will never allow the enemy’s bases in the region to be rebuilt,” Iran’s Fars news agency reported.Former head of Israel’s military intelligence research department and Iran specialist Danny Citrinowicz said in a post on X that "Tehran is not intimidated by the prospect of another confrontation with the United States and Israel.""If attacked, Iran is likely to seek to expand the war from the outset, targeting Gulf states it views as a vulnerable pressure point against Washington.""Tehran is also improving its missile capabilities and preparing its regional partners, including Hezbollah, the Houthis, and Iraqi Shiite militias, for possible involvement," Citrinowicz said."The Iranian leadership believes it can withstand another military campaign, impose significant costs on the United States and its allies, and ultimately force Washington to accept the regime's survival," he added."The central danger is that Washington may envision another short military operation, while Tehran is preparing for a much broader and potentially prolonged regional war."

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Scott Bessent is among current and former US officials being targeted by Iran, according to reports. Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters View image in fullscreen Scott Bessent is among current and former US officials being targeted by Iran, according to reports. Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters US news US Treasury chief Scott Bessent is reportedly latest Trump official to move to military base Bessent, driving force behind US push to cripple Iran’s economy, relocates over alleged threat to his life Staff and agencies Wed 11 Nov 2026 04.11 EST First published on Wed 11 Nov 2026 03.09 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has relocated from his home in the Washington area to a military base after an Iranian threat against his life, the New York Times has reported . Bessent has spearheaded a US push to cripple Iran’s economy since the start of the Middle East war, vowing “economic asphyxiation” of the Islamic republic through a web of sanctions. He is one of a number of senior figures in the Trump administration including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and the new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, to leave their home to live on a military base or protected housing. The US national intelligence chief, Jay Clayton, said last month that Tehran had “substantially increased” its efforts to target Americans in the Middle East and beyond. These include intensifying the targeting of current and former US officials such as Bessent, the NYT reported on Tuesday, citing three sources familiar with the matter. Iranian plotting against US officials has reached a “more advanced stage”, according to the anonymous sources, but the severity of the threats against Bessent was unclear. Washington ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia last month, after increasing attacks from Tehran-backed Houthi fighters. The US military has also removed some aircraft from two British bases in recent weeks amid reported threats from Iran. Hegseth lays it on thick for Trump to shave off fallout from Iran war Read more Diplomatic efforts to end the war are gathering pace, with Rubio saying on Tuesday that the US squeezing of Iran’s economy had made further attacks unnecessary. Bessent has led ‌the US sanctions and economic pressure campaign against Iran, called Operation Economic Outcast, since August to try to ‌push Tehran to end attacks on shipping and reopen the strait of Hormuz. The crucial waterway has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February. The economic pressure campaign, which coincides with a US naval blockade of Iranian ports, has included sanctions on Middle Eastern bank branches and other financial services firms facilitating transactions with Iran. A US Treasury spokesperson said: “The secretary will not be deterred by the Iranian regime’s threats and ‌remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran’s economy.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Thing Our US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion The Times reported that the severity ​of the threats to Bessent was not immediately clear. A source familiar with the matter said security concerns surrounding Bessent had increased when the Wall Street Journal published an aerial view of the Georgetown mansion that Bessent bought for $12.5m (£9.4m) shortly after his confirmation as Treasury secretary in January 2025. The photo allowed Bessent’s home to be geolocated, and Bessent was ⁠relocated to a military base for his safety, the source said, adding: “The news media ​has an obligation to act responsibly ​amid growing threats against public officials.” Iran ​has previously denied plotting to attack officials and people on US soil.
